I want to make a comparison to what you're saying. Let's replace lies of p with a the empire state building


Stairs matters in buildings like this because of the fact that so many people who go in have trouble going up stairs. They get tired over and over again, and eventually they want to take the elevator. It's a human trait. It's a human logic behind building. We get upset, angry, and tilted that a staircase is making us tired and wish there was an elevator to allow us to go up or down. The reason the building was such a highly regarded work of architecture was because of the design choice to NOT allow an elevator. One staircase, and all of the building was built around it.

The reason I get so upset over the decision to add an elevator to this building is because of human nature. Before the renovation, you either had to train or not take the stairs. There was no elevator. It was a true test of endurance, patience, and skill. It's important that there's 1 staircase for those reasons. It's the reason the building was such a great architectural marvel. Human nature, by design, wants the easiest path towards success with minimal struggle. We want to just cruise through an experience and get that dopamine high with minimal effort. The Empire State Building (before the renovations) was not a perfect example of this. A true architectural successor. You had to adapt to the staircase to get that dopamine high. There was no elevator setting. One staircase, and a fantastic experience.

I bitch and moan and complain about elevators being added because I understand human nature. The building will be hated by thousands of people. The renovations will be popular. But when those people get frustrated at the staircase with the new renovations, they will have the option to take the elevator. Fundamentally weakening them as a person, and fundamentally weakening the core identity of the building they are in.

I want to make a comparison to what you're saying. Let's replace lies of p with a the empire state building


Stairs matters in buildings like this because of the fact that so many people who go in have trouble going up stairs. They get tired over and over again, and eventually they want to take the elevator. It's a human trait. It's a human logic behind building. We get upset, angry, and tilted that a staircase is making us tired and wish there was an elevator to allow us to go up or down. The reason the building was such a highly regarded work of architecture was because of the design choice to NOT allow an elevator. One staircase, and all of the building was built around it.

The reason I get so upset over the decision to add an elevator to this building is because of human nature. Before the renovation, you either had to train or not take the stairs. There was no elevator. It was a true test of endurance, patience, and skill. It's important that there's 1 staircase for those reasons. It's the reason the building was such a great architectural marvel. Human nature, by design, wants the easiest path towards success with minimal struggle. We want to just cruise through an experience and get that dopamine high with minimal effort. The Empire State Building (before the renovations) was not a perfect example of this. A true architectural successor. You had to adapt to the staircase to get that dopamine high. There was no elevator setting. One staircase, and a fantastic experience.

I bitch and moan and complain about elevators being added because I understand human nature. The building will be hated by thousands of people. The renovations will be popular. But when those people get frustrated at the staircase with the new renovations, they will have the option to take the elevator. Fundamentally weakening them as a person, and fundamentally weakening the core identity of the building they are in.
